---
title: "Capturing from the web"
subtitle: "One click on any paper page saves it — with its PDF — into FluxLib"
---

You are reading a paper in your browser. One click puts it in your library: the reference, and
the PDF, without a download folder detour or a copy-pasted DOI.

There are two ways to do it. The **extension** is the better one — it captures supplementary
files in the same click and works in Firefox — but it needs a manual install for now. The
**bookmark** needs no install at all and works everywhere except strict-CSP sites in Firefox.

# The extension (recommended)

Build it once:

```bash
node scripts/build-extension.mjs
```

Then load `extension/dist`:

- **Chrome / Edge / Brave** — `chrome://extensions` → **Developer mode** → **Load unpacked**
- **Firefox** — `about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox` → **Load Temporary Add-on…** → pick
  `manifest.json`

::: {.callout-note}
A Firefox temporary add-on is removed when the browser restarts — that's Firefox policy. A
permanent install needs a signed `.xpi`, which Mozilla will issue for free without any public
listing ([self-distribution](https://extensionworkshop.com/documentation/publish/self-distribution/)).
:::

Click the Flux button in the toolbar on any paper page. The badge shows a count when files are
captured, and **supplementary files come with the article in that same click** — SI PDFs,
spreadsheets, videos — each filed against the paper once Flux has identified it.

The extension works where the bookmark can't because its fetches run in a background worker
under host permissions, which a page's Content-Security-Policy does not govern. See
`extension/README.md` for the details.

# The bookmark (no install)

In [Library](../modes/library.qmd), at the bottom of the pane, click **Set up the bookmark…**.
A page opens in your default browser with a green **Add to FluxLib** button. Drag that button
onto your bookmarks bar and you're done — there is nothing to install, no extension, no
account.

::: {.callout-tip}
Bookmarks bar hidden? `Ctrl+Shift+B` (`⌘⇧B` on macOS).
:::

# Using it

Open a paper and click the bookmark. It works on the article page **and** on a PDF you already
have open in the browser. A message appears at the top of the page:

| Message | What happened |
|---|---|
| **Green** — *PDF sent to Flux* | The PDF was captured. Flux files it and matches it to a reference automatically. |
| **Amber** — *Sent details to Flux* | No PDF was reachable, so the paper's details were captured. Flux still adds the reference; it just won't have the PDF yet. |
| Nothing at all | The click didn't run — see [If nothing happens](#if-nothing-happens). |

Captures land in your downloads folder named `flux-…` — the extension puts them in a **`flux/`
subfolder** so a click that grabs an article plus several supplements doesn't scatter files
through your downloads (the bookmark can't do that: `<a download>` cannot name a directory, so
its files land in the root). Either way Flux picks them up within a second or two and removes
them. **Flux doesn't need to be open** — anything captured while it's closed is swept up when
you next start it, and again whenever you switch back to the Flux window. Nothing is lost, and nothing else in your downloads folder is touched: Flux
only ever looks at files it wrote itself.

A captured PDF goes through the same identification as the
[drop folder](../modes/library.qmd#getting-papers-in) — Flux reads the document's own content
(embedded DOI, then the DOI printed on page 1, then its reference list, then a title search) to
find the right reference. It attaches to a paper you already have, or adds the reference if it's
new.

# Why capture from the browser

Flux can already fetch open-access PDFs on its own, and paywalled ones through your
[library proxy](../modes/library.qmd). But some publishers sit behind anti-bot systems —
Cloudflare and PerimeterX — that refuse automated browsers outright, no matter how the request
is dressed up. Those papers are simply unreachable to Flux.

Your browser is not an automated browser. It's you: already signed in, already past the
paywall, already holding the session. So the bookmark captures the PDF *from inside your own
session*, which is why it reaches papers Flux cannot fetch by itself. It's the most capable
acquisition route in the app, and it costs one click.

# Browser support

| Browser | |
|---|---|
| **Chrome, Edge, Brave** | Fully supported. |
| **Safari** | Works. Show the Favourites bar with `⌘⇧B`. |
| **Firefox** | The **extension** works fully. The **bookmark** works on many sites but **silently does nothing on publishers with a strict Content-Security-Policy** — Firefox applies the page's CSP to bookmarklets where Chrome doesn't ([Mozilla bug 866522](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=866522), open since 2013). If a bookmark click does nothing on a publisher site, that's why; use the extension. |

::: {.callout-warning}
You'll find advice to set `security.csp.enable` to `false` in Firefox's `about:config` to make
bookmarklets work. Don't — it disables Content-Security-Policy for **every site you visit**,
which is a real security downgrade. Use Chrome for capture, or save the PDF yourself and drop
it into FluxLib's `pdfs_to_assign` folder.
:::

# If nothing happens

- **Check the address bar** for a blocked-download icon, and allow it.
- **A strict CSP** on the page can block the click outright (see Firefox, above).
- **Some publishers block the PDF fetch but not the script.** You'll get the amber message and
  the reference still arrives — just without its PDF. Flux can often fetch that separately with
  **Get PDFs**.
- **Re-drag the bookmark** after updating Flux: the bookmark holds a copy of the capture code,
  so an old one keeps working the old way. **Set up the bookmark…** always serves the current
  version.

# Where things land

| | |
|---|---|
| Captured files | `<downloads>/flux/` (extension) or the download folder root (bookmark), named `flux-…` |
| Captured PDFs, once filed | `FluxLib/pdfs_to_assign/`, then `FluxLib/items/<citekey>/paper.pdf` |
| Captured supplements | `FluxLib/items/<citekey>/supplements/` (they wait, staged, until the article has been identified) |
| PDFs that couldn't be identified | `FluxLib/pdfs_to_assign/_unresolved/`, with a note saying why |

Nothing is ever guessed: a PDF Flux can't identify with confidence is set aside rather than
attached to the wrong paper.
